=== CALL C0359 ===
Claire: Hiya! Oh, there you are. Can you hear me alright?
Gemma: Yeah, loud and clear. I'm Gemma.
Claire: Claire. Lovely to meet you. I'll be honest, I've sort of forgotten what we're meant to talk about. Did they say?
Gemma: I don't think they said anything. Just chat for three minutes, I think.
Claire: Oh good, I can do that. Did you do that puzzle thing at the start? I got completely stuck on the third one and just stared at it.
Gemma: The shapes one? I quite enjoyed it, to be fair. I worked it out on a bit of paper.
Claire: See, that's organised. I just turned my head sideways a lot. Erm, so where are you calling from?
Gemma: Peterborough. Werrington, on the edge.
Claire: Oh right. I'm in Otley, near Leeds. I saw your dog lead on the hook in your photo, actually. Have you got a dog?
Gemma: Lurcher. Pip.
Claire: No! I've got a lurcher! Biscuit. He's a rescue, very scruffy, steals socks off the radiator and takes them in the garden like trophies.
Gemma: Pip ate a tea towel last week.
Claire: A whole tea towel?
Gemma: Most of it. Vet said just keep an eye, and it came out the other end fine. Not the nicest Saturday morning, mind.
Claire: Oh god. They're daft, aren't they? Lovely, but daft. Do you take her out much?
Gemma: Ferry Meadows most days. I do the parkrun there on Saturdays as well, so she gets dragged round after.
Claire: Ooh, a parkrun. I'm not a runner. I walk Biscuit up the Chevin, which is a big hill above Otley, and that's about as athletic as I get. I do the wild swimming in summer, but that's mostly standing in a river going "it's freezing, it's freezing" for ten minutes.
Gemma: Rather you than me, honestly. What do you do for work, then?
Claire: Speech and language therapist, with kids. NHS, so I go round clinics and primary schools in Leeds three days a week. Mostly little ones who aren't talking yet, or not very clearly, and you play with them on the floor and try to work out what's going on. And then I go home and don't do my paperwork, which is the bit I'm terrible at. Sorry, that's a lot. What about you?
Gemma: Quality engineer. We make engines and generators. When a supplier sends us parts that fail inspection, I'm the one who works out why, and then I sit in a meeting with them while they try to tell me it's not their fault.
Claire: Oh, I bet you're good at that.
Gemma: I just keep asking for the data. They give up eventually.
Claire: Ha! I love that. Did you go to uni for it, or...?
Gemma: Apprenticeship at sixteen, then college on day release, then I did my degree part-time at night in my late twenties. Work paid.
Claire: At night, while working? That's proper graft. I started an MA once and dropped it after a year because I kept reading the interesting bits instead of doing the essays.
Gemma: That's the trouble with interesting bits, to be fair.
Claire: Exactly! Do you know what I mean, you go off down a rabbit hole and suddenly it's March. Sorry, where was I?
Gemma: Your MA, which you didn't finish.
Claire: Ha, yes, thank you. One day, I keep telling Mark that.

=== CALL C0360 ===
Callum: Alright, boss! Can you hear me?
Martin: Yes, I can, thank you. Hello. I'm Martin.
Callum: Callum. Nice one. Sorry if it's loud, there's a nail bar under my flat and they've got the music going already.
Martin: Ah. I did wonder what the bass line was.
Callum: Every day, from nine. You get used to it, kind of. So where are you, then?
Martin: Lewes, in Sussex. And you're in London, I'd guess?
Callum: Catford, South East. Proper London, not like where I grew up out in Orpington, innit.
Martin: Right. I grew up in Maidstone, so I'll take your word on the distinction.
Callum: Ha, nah, Maidstone's fine. So what d'you do?
Martin: I'm a structural engineer. Mostly old bridges, and old masonry generally. People ring us when a Victorian arch has got a crack in it and they want to know whether to worry.
Callum: And do they have to worry?
Martin: Well, er, usually less than they think. Old bridges are often in better shape than they look, which is sort of the fun of it. You find odd repairs somebody made in the twenties and you try to work out what they were thinking.
Callum: That's actually sick, like, detective stuff.
Martin: That's the bit I like, yes. What about you?
Callum: I'm doing media and comms at uni, second year. It's basically media strategy. And I do production work on the side, events, warehouse parties, setting up rigs, lights, sound, all that.
Martin: That sounds like quite hard work.
Callum: Nah, it's a laugh, mostly. Long nights, though. The idea is music or events marketing after, running campaigns for a label or whatever. Got loads of contacts from doing it, you get me.
Martin: Mm. Have you got anything lined up, placements and so on?
Callum: Erm, not yet, not like official. It's more of a who-you-know thing in that world, innit. It'll sort itself out.
Martin: I'm sure. Sorry, I meant to ask, is that an Oldboy poster behind you? In your photo, I think.
Callum: Yes! You know Oldboy?
Martin: Only because my son made me watch it years ago. The corridor scene with the hammer, I think it was.
Callum: The corridor scene, mate! One take. People go on about it being violent, but nah, nah, see, the thing is, it's actually about guilt, the whole film. Everyone misses that.
Martin: That's fair. I read a lot of translated novels, and there's often that sort of thing, the story's dressed as one thing and it's really about something else entirely.
Callum: Exactly, that's exactly it. What've you read, then, like Korean stuff?
Martin: A bit. I've just finished a Han Kang, The Vegetarian. I'm not sure I understood all of it, to be honest, but I kept thinking about it for weeks.
Callum: See, that's the sign it's good, innit, when it stays with you.
Martin: I'd agree with that. Do you get much time for films, with the course and the events work?
Callum: Too much, if I'm honest. Watched one last night instead of doing an essay, so, you know.
Martin: Well, er, I've done much the same with drawings instead of reports. I won't tell anyone if you don't.
Callum: Deal, boss. So how long have you been doing bridges, then, like—

=== CALL C0361 ===
Gemma: Hiya. Can you hear me okay?
Kerry: Yeah, fine. I'm Kerry.
Gemma: Gemma. Is this your first one?
Kerry: First one, yeah. I was sat on my own last round. Have you done one already?
Gemma: Just the one, with a woman called Claire. Lovely, talked a lot. So where are you?
Kerry: Washington. Near Sunderland, not the American one.
Gemma: I'd assumed. I'm Peterborough.
Kerry: Right. Never been.
Gemma: Not many people have, to be fair. It's got a cathedral and a lot of roundabouts. What do you do?
Kerry: Team leader at a contact centre. Broadband and TV. I've got fourteen advisors and I take the escalations, so anyone who's really kicking off gets put through to me.
Gemma: Do you get a lot of that?
Kerry: Loads at the minute, with the price rises. People ring up shouting before you've said hello. You just let them get it out, to be honest. Most of them calm down once they've had their rant and they know you're actually going to sort it.
Gemma: I'd be rubbish at that. I'd want to argue back.
Kerry: Nah, you can't. What about you?
Gemma: Quality engineer at an engine manufacturer. Parts come in, fail inspection, I find out why. Lots of spreadsheets and suppliers telling me it's not their fault.
Kerry: Sounds like my job but with engines.
Gemma: Ha, it probably is, to be fair. Someone's always blaming someone else.
Kerry: That's every job, isn't it. I can't stand it when people make excuses instead of just saying they got it wrong.
Gemma: Same. Just tell me what happened and we'll fix it, yeah?
Kerry: Exactly. Is that a dog lead on your door in your photo? I clocked it.
Gemma: Yeah, Pip, she's a lurcher. You had a dog bed in yours.
Kerry: Tia. Staffy. She's eaten two settee cushions this year.
Gemma: Pip ate a tea towel last week. Most of one.
Kerry: Was she alright?
Gemma: Fine. Came out the other end.
Kerry: They're daft. Tia's soft as anything, though. People see a staffy and cross the road.
Gemma: Do you get out with her much?
Kerry: Most nights, round the wetland centre after work. That's my exercise, to be honest. Tried a gym once, bored stiff.
Gemma: I do parkrun and five-a-side, but I'm a bit of a nutter about it. My partner thinks I'm mad.
Kerry: What's his name?
Gemma: Dean.
Kerry: You're joking. Mine's Dean.
Gemma: No way. What does yours do?
Kerry: Plasterer. Self-employed.
Gemma: Mine's a self-employed electrician. That's a bit weird, isn't it.
Kerry: Bit, yeah. Has yours done that plaster behind you? That half-done bit in your photo?
Gemma: No, that's me. I'm doing the spare room. Dean's useless with a hawk and trowel.
Kerry: See, mine'd have that done in an afternoon. I'm doing ours up as well, really slowly. Been about two years.
Gemma: Ha. Do you want kids, you two, or is it a spare spare room?
Kerry: Erm... sorry, what d'you mean, like is it a nursery?
Gemma: Yeah, sort of. Sorry, that's nosy.
Kerry: Nah, you're alright. Just a spare room at the minute. Dean's keener than me, to be honest. We'll see.
Gemma: Fair enough. We've mostly decided not to. My mum's not thrilled.
Kerry: My mam'd be the same. She'd have it decorated for me.
Gemma: Ha, mine drops hints over Sunday dinner.
Kerry: We have Sunday tea at my mam's most weeks, so I get it with the roast potatoes.

=== CALL C0362 ===
Claire: Hello! Oh, hiya. Can you hear me?
Callum: Yeah, yeah, all good. Callum. Sorry about the music, there's a nail bar under my flat.
Claire: Oh, I can just hear a bit of bass. I'm Claire. Don't worry, I've had worse. My son used to play drum and bass at two in the morning.
Callum: Proper. How old is he?
Claire: Joe's twenty, he's at uni in Glasgow. You actually remind me of him a bit, from your photo. The clothes rail especially. He's got a rail exactly like that, I don't think he's ever hung anything on it.
Callum: Ha! Nah, mine's organised chaos, you get me. Everything on there's from Depop, though. Got a jacket last week for fifteen quid.
Claire: Fifteen quid! I love a charity shop. I go round Otley and Ilkley on my days off. Erm, so what do you do, Callum?
Callum: I'm at uni as well, media and comms, second year. Plus I do events stuff on the side, production, warehouse parties.
Claire: Oh, that sounds fun. Joe would love that. Is it fun, or is it just carrying things?
Callum: Bit of both, ngl. Mostly carrying speakers at four in the morning. But it's contacts, innit. That's what counts in that world.
Claire: That's true, I suppose. What sort of thing do you want to do after?
Callum: Music marketing, campaigns, that kind of thing. Or start my own night with mates.
Claire: Ooh, a club night. What would you call it?
Callum: Erm... haven't got that far, to be honest. Working on it.
Claire: Ha, that's the hardest bit. I'd spend six months on the name and never book the venue. I've got that poster too, haven't I, in your photo? The film, Oldboy?
Callum: Yeah, Oldboy, Korean. The bloke I just talked to, Martin, he'd seen it as well, which I wasn't expecting.
Claire: The engineer one? He looked very sensible. Reminded me of my husband.
Callum: He was alright, actually. Knows his books. Do you watch Korean stuff?
Claire: Not really films, but I've been on a big Korean food kick. I've got a jar of gochujang in the fridge and I'm learning a bit of Korean on an app, on and off. Mostly off. I tried a kimchi stew last week and it went a bit wrong, sort of, it was more like a sad orange soup.
Callum: Nah, see, the thing is, you need the old kimchi for that, the proper sour stuff. Fresh kimchi doesn't work.
Claire: Is that it? Oh, that makes sense actually. I used it straight out the jar. Do you cook, then?
Callum: Erm, not really. I eat, mostly. There's a decent Korean place in Peckham, though, I'll be honest.
Claire: Ha! That's very Joe. He only rings when he needs money or wants to know how long you cook rice for.
Callum: Twenty minutes, tell him. Is it boring, being a speech therapist? Sorry, that came out wrong.
Claire: No, no, it's not boring at all! It's lovely. Little ones who aren't talking yet, and you get down on the floor with a bag of toys and suddenly they say "bus" and you're chuffed for a week.
Callum: That's actually nice, that.
Claire: It is. The paperwork's awful, mind, I'm hopeless at it. Do you get your essays done on time?
Callum: Yeah, no, definitely. Mostly. Kind of.
Claire: Ha, that's a no, love. Joe says exactly that.
Callum: Okay, okay, I resubmitted two last year. Don't tell my lecturer—

=== CALL C0363 ===
Callum: Alright! Can you hear me? Sorry about the music, there's a nail bar downstairs.
Gemma: Yeah, I can hear it a bit. I'm Gemma.
Callum: Callum. Where you calling from?
Gemma: Peterborough. You?
Callum: Catford, South London. Peterborough, that's the Posh, innit? Football.
Gemma: That's us. I go a few times a season with my partner and my brother. Who d'you support?
Callum: Palace. Mostly from the pub, to be fair. Selhurst tickets aren't cheap.
Gemma: Do you play at all?
Callum: Used to do five-a-side on Thursdays. Packed it in, though. Fell out with the bloke running it, proper jobsworth, you get me.
Gemma: Ha. I play Wednesdays, mixed league. I'm probably the jobsworth in ours, to be fair. I keep the score.
Callum: Nah, keeping score's fine. He used to fine you a quid for being late. Who does that?
Gemma: Sounds sensible to me. Were you late a lot?
Callum: Couple of times. Southeastern, innit, the trains are a joke. Anyway. What d'you do?
Gemma: Quality engineer. Engines and generators. When parts come in wrong, I find out why.
Callum: Like an investigator.
Gemma: Sort of. Lot of spreadsheets. Lot of asking people for the data until they give it me. What about you?
Callum: Media and comms at uni, second year. And production work on the side, events. Setting up rigs for warehouse parties, lights, sound, all that.
Gemma: Is that paid, or just helping mates?
Callum: Paid. Cash, mostly. It's more about the contacts, though. I want to get into music marketing, running campaigns for labels, that kind of thing.
Gemma: Have you applied for anything?
Callum: Erm, not yet. Everyone keeps asking me that today, honestly. Martin asked, Claire asked.
Gemma: Probably because it's the obvious question, to be fair. I'm not having a go.
Callum: Nah, I know, I know. It's just, that world's not like engineering. You don't fill in a form. You know someone who knows someone.
Gemma: We've got a placement lad at work, actually, media degree, doing our internal comms. He got it through his uni careers service. Might be worth a look, yeah?
Callum: Yeah, maybe. Sound. So what d'you do for fun, apart from bossing people about at football?
Gemma: Parkrun on Saturdays, the dog, pub quiz. And one proper holiday a year. I did Iceland for my fortieth.
Callum: Iceland's sick. I went to a festival in Croatia a couple of years back. Stuck it on a credit card, still paying it off, ha.
Gemma: That's the thing with festivals. I'd have done a spreadsheet first.
Callum: A spreadsheet? For a holiday?
Gemma: Every year. Budget, flights, what the dog costs in kennels. Dean thinks I'm mad.
Callum: Nah, that's actually smart, ngl. I want to do Vietnam and Thailand properly. Once the loan comes in.
Gemma: Go in the summer, so you're not missing lectures. And price it up first.
Callum: Yes, boss. That half-done plaster in your photo, though, that was stressing me out.
Gemma: Ha! That's my spare room. I'm doing it myself. It'll be done when it's done.
Callum: You plaster? Fair play.
Gemma: Badly, but yeah. It's cheaper than paying someone, and I quite like it.

=== CALL C0364 ===
Callum: Alright! Can you hear me okay? Sorry if there's music, there's a nail bar under my flat.
Kerry: Yeah, I can hear it. I'm Kerry.
Callum: Callum. Where are you, then?
Kerry: Washington. Near Sunderland.
Callum: Oh, proper north. I'm Catford, South London. What d'you do?
Kerry: Team leader at a contact centre. Broadband and TV.
Callum: Is that the lanyard in your photo? Sorry, I clocked it, I thought you were still at work.
Kerry: I'd just got in from a shift, to be honest. I forget I've got it on half the time.
Callum: Long shifts, then?
Kerry: Fifty, fifty-five hours some weeks with overtime. I've got fourteen advisors and I take all the escalations, so when somebody's shouting they get put through to me.
Callum: Nah, I couldn't do that. I'd just hang up on them.
Kerry: You can't hang up. You let them have their rant, then you sort it. Most people just want to know somebody's actually listening.
Callum: Fair. That's kind of like events, though, innit. Someone's always kicking off about the sound or the guest list, and you've got to keep it calm.
Kerry: What events?
Callum: I do production work. Warehouse parties, setting up the rigs, lights, all that. And I'm at uni, media and comms.
Kerry: Right. Is that full-time, the uni?
Callum: Yeah, second year. Well, full-time on paper, you get me.
Kerry: Meaning you don't go.
Callum: Ha, nah, I go! Mostly. Some of the lectures are a bit dead, to be fair.
Kerry: I've got lads like that at work. Always a reason why they've not done it.
Callum: Nah, nah, see, the thing is, that's different. If it's a job you've got to turn up, obviously. Uni's more, like, you're paying, so it's your choice.
Kerry: Still your money, though, isn't it. I left college in my second year to go full-time, so I'm not one to talk, to be honest.
Callum: What were you doing?
Kerry: BTEC in business, at Sunderland College. I needed the wage. I did my NVQ through work after.
Callum: See, that's what I'm saying, you don't need the degree to do alright. You're a manager now.
Kerry: Team leader. It's not the same money, believe me. I'm after operations manager in a few years.
Callum: You'll get it. You've got the vibe.
Kerry: What vibe?
Callum: Like, nobody's messing you about.
Kerry: Ha. Fair enough. What do you do when you're not at parties, then?
Callum: Films, mostly. Korean thrillers, that kind of thing. Making beats. You?
Kerry: Reality telly. Married at First Sight, Love Island. Crime documentaries on Netflix.
Callum: Oh, the crime ones are decent, actually. Which ones?
Kerry: Whatever's new, to be honest. I'm not fussy. I walk the dog and I watch telly, that's about it.
Callum: What dog?
Kerry: Staffy, Tia. She eats the settee.
Callum: Staffies are sound. Everyone thinks they're scary.
Kerry: Soft as anything, she is.

=== CALL C0365 ===
Claire: Hiya! Oh, hello, it's you. I said you looked like my husband, I hope you don't mind.
Martin: Hello. I'm Martin. I'll take that as a compliment, I think.
Claire: You should, he's very sensible. I'm Claire. I'm in Otley, near Leeds.
Martin: Oh, our son lives in Leeds. Headingley, I think it's called.
Claire: Headingley, yes, lots of students and cricket. We're just up the road from there. Where are you?
Martin: Lewes, in East Sussex. I noticed the postcard from Lisbon in your photo, actually. I'm learning Portuguese at the moment, rather slowly.
Claire: No! I love Lisbon. We went a few years ago, all those hills and the little yellow trams, and I just kept ordering custard tarts and pretending it was lunch. Why Portuguese?
Martin: Well, er, I walked part of the Camino through Portugal and felt a bit foolish only having Italian. So there's an app, and a conversation group on a Wednesday night where I mostly apologise.
Claire: Ha, that's me with my Korean. I'm learning it on an app, on and off, mostly off. What do you do, Martin? I've been told by Callum you know your books.
Martin: Have you? That's kind of him. I'm a structural engineer, mostly old bridges and masonry. People send for us when a Victorian arch has cracked and they'd like to know whether it's going to fall down.
Claire: And is it?
Martin: Usually not. They're more forgiving than people think. What about you?
Claire: Speech and language therapist, NHS, with little ones. So I'm sort of on the floor with toy buses all day trying to get a shy four-year-old to say anything at all. And I love it. The paperwork, less so.
Martin: I'm the same with reports. The interesting part is out on site. The writing up is where it all goes wrong.
Claire: Yes! Do you know what I mean, you've done the actual thing, why do I have to write it all down as well. Sorry. Is that a piano behind you, in your photo?
Martin: My wife Helen's. She teaches music. I don't play, I just get told when I'm humming flat.
Claire: Oh, I sing alto in a choir in Leeds, and I'm terrible at learning my parts. We've got a concert soon and there's one bit I just cannot get, I come in a bar early every single time.
Martin: Helen would say count, and then count again.
Claire: Everyone says that! I'm sure she's right. Erm, I saw your sketch of a bridge, too. Did you do that?
Martin: I did, yes. That's the one at Barcombe, near us. I draw them partly for work and partly for the pleasure of it.
Claire: That's lovely. I do lino prints, the heron and the hare on my board are mine, so the kitchen table's always covered in ink.
Martin: I thought they were rather good, actually. I wondered whether you'd bought them.
Claire: Oh, stop, you'll make me blush. Do you cook? Mark does the Sunday roast, but I do tea in the week, whatever comes in the veg box.
Martin: I do most of our dinners. I tried a Sri Lankan curry last week from a borrowed book. It was nearly right.
Claire: Nearly right is my whole cooking career, love.

=== CALL C0366 ===
Claire: Hiya! Oh, hello. Can you hear me alright?
Kerry: Yeah, fine. I'm Kerry.
Claire: Claire. I'm in Otley, near Leeds. Are you up north as well? I'm guessing from the voice.
Kerry: Washington, near Sunderland.
Claire: Oh, lovely. I had a friend at uni from Sunderland, she used to call everyone "pet" and I was so jealous. What do you do?
Kerry: Team leader at a contact centre. Broadband and TV complaints, mostly. I've got fourteen on my team.
Claire: Fourteen! That's a lot of people to keep an eye on.

Kerry: Tia. Staffy. She's eating the settee cushions one at a time.

Claire: Mostly. She's tougher than me. Anyway! Do you do anything arty? I've got ink all over my hands from lino printing.
Kerry: Not really. I've never even been to the Baltic and it's half an hour away.
Claire: Oh, you should go, it's free, and there's a—
Kerry: I know, everyone says.

=== CALL C0367 ===
Gemma: Hiya. Can you hear me?
Martin: Yes, perfectly, thank you. I'm Martin.
Gemma: Gemma. Peterborough. You're the engineer, I think? Claire mentioned.
Martin: That's me, yes. Structural, mostly historic bridges. And you're in quality, I gather?
Gemma: Quality engineer. Engines and generators. Supplier stuff, root cause when parts fail inspection.
Martin: Ah, so you're the detective at your end too. That's the bit of my job I like best, working out why something's gone wrong, or in my case why it hasn't.
Gemma: Same. Most people hate it. I quite like sitting a supplier down and just asking for the data until it comes out.
Martin: Well, er, I suspect you're better at that than I am. I tend to give people the benefit of the doubt for a bit too long.
Gemma: I give them about one meeting, to be fair. Did you do engineering at uni, then?
Martin: Bristol, a very long time ago. Nineteen eighty-four. What about you?
Gemma: Apprenticeship at sixteen, machining. Then BTEC, HNC on day release, and a part-time BEng in my late twenties. Nights, while working full-time.
Martin: That's a lot harder than the way I did it, you know. I just turned up at eighteen and somebody else paid.
Gemma: Ha. It was alright. My dad used to tell everyone at the club about it.
Martin: I'm sure he did. He must have been very proud.
Gemma: He was. He passed four years ago. So, I noticed the books behind you in your photo. Proper reference books.
Martin: Some of them are older than I am. And I noticed your plastering, actually. Is that your own work?
Gemma: It is. Spare room. Half done. Everyone's mentioned it today, Callum said it was stressing him out.
Martin: Ha. I'm trying to fix a sash window in our back bedroom at the moment, and it's been about four months, so I'm in no position to judge.
Gemma: Is it the cords?
Martin: Partly the cords, partly about a hundred years of paint holding it shut. I've got as far as taking the beading off and then sort of stalled.
Gemma: That's the worst bit, to be fair. Once it's open you just crack on.
Martin: That's what my wife says. What do you do outside work, then?
Gemma: Five-a-side Wednesdays, parkrun Saturdays at Ferry Meadows, the dog. I keep a log of my times. I'm a bit sad about it.
Martin: Not at all. I've got a sourdough starter I keep notes on, and I'm convinced Helen's feeding it behind my back because it's doing far better than it should.
Gemma: Have you asked her?
Martin: She denies everything.
Gemma: You need a controlled trial. Mark the jar.
Martin: That's a genuinely good idea. I'll put a line on it tonight with a pen.
Gemma: Then you'll have data. Do you walk much? You look like you're outdoors a lot.
Martin: The South Downs, most Saturday mornings. I saw a red kite last weekend over—

calls.C0359:
Claire: Hiya! Oh, there you are. Can you hear me alright?
Gemma: Yeah, loud and clear. I'm Gemma.
Claire: Claire. Lovely to meet you. I'll be honest, I've sort of forgotten what we're meant to talk about. Did they say?
Gemma: I don't think they said anything. Just chat for three minutes, I think.
Claire: Oh good, I can do that. Did you do that puzzle thing at the start? I got completely stuck on the third one and just stared at it.
Gemma: The shapes one? I quite enjoyed it, to be fair. I worked it out on a bit of paper.
Claire: See, that's organised. I just turned my head sideways a lot. Erm, so where are you calling from?
Gemma: Peterborough. Werrington, on the edge.
Claire: Oh right. I'm in Otley, near Leeds. I saw your dog lead on the hook in your photo, actually. Have you got a dog?
Gemma: Lurcher. Pip.
Claire: No! I've got a lurcher! Biscuit. He's a rescue, very scruffy, steals socks off the radiator and takes them in the garden like trophies.
Gemma: Pip ate a tea towel last week.
Claire: A whole tea towel?
Gemma: Most of it. Vet said just keep an eye, and it came out the other end fine. Not the nicest Saturday morning, mind.
Claire: Oh god. They're daft, aren't they? Lovely, but daft. Do you take her out much?
Gemma: Ferry Meadows most days. I do the parkrun there on Saturdays as well, so she gets dragged round after.
Claire: Ooh, a parkrun. I'm not a runner. I walk Biscuit up the Chevin, which is a big hill above Otley, and that's about as athletic as I get. I do the wild swimming in summer, but that's mostly standing in a river going "it's freezing, it's freezing" for ten minutes.
Gemma: Rather you than me, honestly. What do you do for work, then?
Claire: Speech and language therapist, with kids. NHS, so I go round clinics and primary schools in Leeds three days a week. Mostly little ones who aren't talking yet, or not very clearly, and you play with them on the floor and try to work out what's going on. And then I go home and don't do my paperwork, which is the bit I'm terrible at. Sorry, that's a lot. What about you?
Gemma: Quality engineer. We make engines and generators. When a supplier sends us parts that fail inspection, I'm the one who works out why, and then I sit in a meeting with them while they try to tell me it's not their fault.
Claire: Oh, I bet you're good at that.
Gemma: I just keep asking for the data. They give up eventually.
Claire: Ha! I love that. Did you go to uni for it, or...?
Gemma: Apprenticeship at sixteen, then college on day release, then I did my degree part-time at night in my late twenties. Work paid.
Claire: At night, while working? That's proper graft. I started an MA once and dropped it after a year because I kept reading the interesting bits instead of doing the essays.
Gemma: That's the trouble with interesting bits, to be fair.
Claire: Exactly! Do you know what I mean, you go off down a rabbit hole and suddenly it's March. Sorry, where was I?
Gemma: Your MA, which you didn't finish.
Claire: Ha, yes, thank you. One day, I keep telling Mark that.
calls.C0360:
Callum: Alright, boss! Can you hear me?
Martin: Yes, I can, thank you. Hello. I'm Martin.
Callum: Callum. Nice one. Sorry if it's loud, there's a nail bar under my flat and they've got the music going already.
Martin: Ah. I did wonder what the bass line was.
Callum: Every day, from nine. You get used to it, kind of. So where are you, then?
Martin: Lewes, in Sussex. And you're in London, I'd guess?
Callum: Catford, South East. Proper London, not like where I grew up out in Orpington, innit.
Martin: Right. I grew up in Maidstone, so I'll take your word on the distinction.
Callum: Ha, nah, Maidstone's fine. So what d'you do?
Martin: I'm a structural engineer. Mostly old bridges, and old masonry generally. People ring us when a Victorian arch has got a crack in it and they want to know whether to worry.
Callum: And do they have to worry?
Martin: Well, er, usually less than they think. Old bridges are often in better shape than they look, which is sort of the fun of it. You find odd repairs somebody made in the twenties and you try to work out what they were thinking.
Callum: That's actually sick, like, detective stuff.
Martin: That's the bit I like, yes. What about you?
Callum: I'm doing media and comms at uni, second year. It's basically media strategy. And I do production work on the side, events, warehouse parties, setting up rigs, lights, sound, all that.
Martin: That sounds like quite hard work.
Callum: Nah, it's a laugh, mostly. Long nights, though. The idea is music or events marketing after, running campaigns for a label or whatever. Got loads of contacts from doing it, you get me.
Martin: Mm. Have you got anything lined up, placements and so on?
Callum: Erm, not yet, not like official. It's more of a who-you-know thing in that world, innit. It'll sort itself out.
Martin: I'm sure. Sorry, I meant to ask, is that an Oldboy poster behind you? In your photo, I think.
Callum: Yes! You know Oldboy?
Martin: Only because my son made me watch it years ago. The corridor scene with the hammer, I think it was.
Callum: The corridor scene, mate! One take. People go on about it being violent, but nah, nah, see, the thing is, it's actually about guilt, the whole film. Everyone misses that.
Martin: That's fair. I read a lot of translated novels, and there's often that sort of thing, the story's dressed as one thing and it's really about something else entirely.
Callum: Exactly, that's exactly it. What've you read, then, like Korean stuff?
Martin: A bit. I've just finished a Han Kang, The Vegetarian. I'm not sure I understood all of it, to be honest, but I kept thinking about it for weeks.
Callum: See, that's the sign it's good, innit, when it stays with you.
Martin: I'd agree with that. Do you get much time for films, with the course and the events work?
Callum: Too much, if I'm honest. Watched one last night instead of doing an essay, so, you know.
Martin: Well, er, I've done much the same with drawings instead of reports. I won't tell anyone if you don't.
Callum: Deal, boss. So how long have you been doing bridges, then, like—
calls.C0361:
Gemma: Hiya. Can you hear me okay?
Kerry: Yeah, fine. I'm Kerry.

Kerry: First one, yeah. I was sat on my own last round. Have you done one already?

Kerry: Right. Never been.

Gemma: Do you get a lot of that?
Kerry: Loads at the minute, with the price rises. People ring up shouting before you've said hello. You just let them get it out, to be honest. Most of them calm down once they've had their rant and they know you're actually going to sort it.
Gemma: I'd be rubbish at that. I'd want to argue back.
Kerry: Nah, you can't. What about you?
Gemma: Quality engineer at an engine manufacturer. Parts come in, fail inspection, I find out why. Lots of spreadsheets and suppliers telling me it's not their fault.
Kerry: Sounds like my job but with engines.
Gemma: Ha, it probably is, to be fair. Someone's always blaming someone else.
Kerry: That's every job, isn't it. I can't stand it when people make excuses instead of just saying they got it wrong.
Gemma: Same. Just tell me what happened and we'll fix it, yeah?
Kerry: Exactly. Is that a dog lead on your door in your photo? I clocked it.
Gemma: Yeah, Pip, she's a lurcher. You had a dog bed in yours.
Kerry: Tia. Staffy. She's eaten two settee cushions this year.
Gemma: Pip ate a tea towel last week. Most of one.
Kerry: Was she alright?
Gemma: Fine. Came out the other end.
Kerry: They're daft. Tia's soft as anything, though. People see a staffy and cross the road.
Gemma: Do you get out with her much?
Kerry: Most nights, round the wetland centre after work. That's my exercise, to be honest. Tried a gym once, bored stiff.
Gemma: I do parkrun and five-a-side, but I'm a bit of a nutter about it. My partner thinks I'm mad.
Kerry: What's his name?
Gemma: Dean.
Kerry: You're joking. Mine's Dean.
Gemma: No way. What does yours do?
Kerry: Plasterer. Self-employed.
Gemma: Mine's a self-employed electrician. That's a bit weird, isn't it.
Kerry: Bit, yeah. Has yours done that plaster behind you? That half-done bit in your photo?
Gemma: No, that's me. I'm doing the spare room. Dean's useless with a hawk and trowel.
Kerry: See, mine'd have that done in an afternoon. I'm doing ours up as well, really slowly. Been about two years.
Gemma: Ha. Do you want kids, you two, or is it a spare spare room?
Kerry: Erm... sorry, what d'you mean, like is it a nursery?
Gemma: Yeah, sort of. Sorry, that's nosy.
Kerry: Nah, you're alright. Just a spare room at the minute. Dean's keener than me, to be honest. We'll see.
Gemma: Fair enough. We've mostly decided not to. My mum's not thrilled.
Kerry: My mam'd be the same. She'd have it decorated for me.
Gemma: Ha, mine drops hints over Sunday dinner.
Kerry: We have Sunday tea at my mam's most weeks, so I get it with the roast potatoes.
calls.C0362:
Claire: Hello! Oh, hiya. Can you hear me?
Callum: Yeah, yeah, all good. Callum. Sorry about the music, there's a nail bar under my flat.
Claire: Oh, I can just hear a bit of bass. I'm Claire. Don't worry, I've had worse. My son used to play drum and bass at two in the morning.
Callum: Proper. How old is he?
Claire: Joe's twenty, he's at uni in Glasgow. You actually remind me of him a bit, from your photo. The clothes rail especially. He's got a rail exactly like that, I don't think he's ever hung anything on it.
Callum: Ha! Nah, mine's organised chaos, you get me. Everything on there's from Depop, though. Got a jacket last week for fifteen quid.
Claire: Fifteen quid! I love a charity shop. I go round Otley and Ilkley on my days off. Erm, so what do you do, Callum?
Callum: I'm at uni as well, media and comms, second year. Plus I do events stuff on the side, production, warehouse parties.
Claire: Oh, that sounds fun. Joe would love that. Is it fun, or is it just carrying things?
Callum: Bit of both, ngl. Mostly carrying speakers at four in the morning. But it's contacts, innit. That's what counts in that world.
Claire: That's true, I suppose. What sort of thing do you want to do after?
Callum: Music marketing, campaigns, that kind of thing. Or start my own night with mates.
Claire: Ooh, a club night. What would you call it?
Callum: Erm... haven't got that far, to be honest. Working on it.
Claire: Ha, that's the hardest bit. I'd spend six months on the name and never book the venue. I've got that poster too, haven't I, in your photo? The film, Oldboy?
Callum: Yeah, Oldboy, Korean. The bloke I just talked to, Martin, he'd seen it as well, which I wasn't expecting.
Claire: The engineer one? He looked very sensible. Reminded me of my husband.
Callum: He was alright, actually. Knows his books. Do you watch Korean stuff?
Claire: Not really films, but I've been on a big Korean food kick. I've got a jar of gochujang in the fridge and I'm learning a bit of Korean on an app, on and off. Mostly off. I tried a kimchi stew last week and it went a bit wrong, sort of, it was more like a sad orange soup.
Callum: Nah, see, the thing is, you need the old kimchi for that, the proper sour stuff. Fresh kimchi doesn't work.
Claire: Is that it? Oh, that makes sense actually. I used it straight out the jar. Do you cook, then?
Callum: Erm, not really. I eat, mostly. There's a decent Korean place in Peckham, though, I'll be honest.
Claire: Ha! That's very Joe. He only rings when he needs money or wants to know how long you cook rice for.
Callum: Twenty minutes, tell him. Is it boring, being a speech therapist? Sorry, that came out wrong.
Claire: No, no, it's not boring at all! It's lovely. Little ones who aren't talking yet, and you get down on the floor with a bag of toys and suddenly they say "bus" and you're chuffed for a week.
Callum: That's actually nice, that.
Claire: It is. The paperwork's awful, mind, I'm hopeless at it. Do you get your essays done on time?
Callum: Yeah, no, definitely. Mostly. Kind of.
Claire: Ha, that's a no, love. Joe says exactly that.
Callum: Okay, okay, I resubmitted two last year. Don't tell my lecturer—
calls.C0363:
Callum: Alright! Can you hear me? Sorry about the music, there's a nail bar downstairs.
Gemma: Yeah, I can hear it a bit. I'm Gemma.
Callum: Callum. Where you calling from?

Gemma: Quality engineer. Engines and generators. When parts come in wrong, I find out why.
Callum: Like an investigator.

Callum: Media and comms at uni, second year. And production work on the side, events. Setting up rigs for warehouse parties, lights, sound, all that.

Gemma: Have you applied for anything?
Callum: Erm, not yet. Everyone keeps asking me that today, honestly. Martin asked, Claire asked.
Gemma: Probably because it's the obvious question, to be fair. I'm not having a go.
Callum: Nah, I know, I know. It's just, that world's not like engineering. You don't fill in a form. You know someone who knows someone.
Gemma: We've got a placement lad at work, actually, media degree, doing our internal comms. He got it through his uni careers service. Might be worth a look, yeah?
Callum: Yeah, maybe. Sound. So what d'you do for fun, apart from bossing people about at football?
Gemma: Parkrun on Saturdays, the dog, pub quiz. And one proper holiday a year. I did Iceland for my fortieth.

Gemma: Every year. Budget, flights, what the dog costs in kennels. Dean thinks I'm mad.

Gemma: Go in the summer, so you're not missing lectures. And price it up first.
Callum: Yes, boss. That half-done plaster in your photo, though, that was stressing me out.

Callum: You plaster? Fair play.
Gemma: Badly, but yeah. It's cheaper than paying someone, and I quite like it.
calls.C0364:

Kerry: What vibe?

Kerry: Ha. Fair enough. What do you do when you're not at parties, then?

calls.C0365:
Claire: Hiya! Oh, hello, it's you. I said you looked like my husband, I hope you don't mind.
Martin: Hello. I'm Martin. I'll take that as a compliment, I think.
Claire: You should, he's very sensible. I'm Claire. I'm in Otley, near Leeds.
Martin: Oh, our son lives in Leeds. Headingley, I think it's called.
Claire: Headingley, yes, lots of students and cricket. We're just up the road from there. Where are you?
Martin: Lewes, in East Sussex. I noticed the postcard from Lisbon in your photo, actually. I'm learning Portuguese at the moment, rather slowly.
Claire: No! I love Lisbon. We went a few years ago, all those hills and the little yellow trams, and I just kept ordering custard tarts and pretending it was lunch. Why Portuguese?
Martin: Well, er, I walked part of the Camino through Portugal and felt a bit foolish only having Italian. So there's an app, and a conversation group on a Wednesday night where I mostly apologise.
Claire: Ha, that's me with my Korean. I'm learning it on an app, on and off, mostly off. What do you do, Martin? I've been told by Callum you know your books.
Martin: Have you? That's kind of him. I'm a structural engineer, mostly old bridges and masonry. People send for us when a Victorian arch has cracked and they'd like to know whether it's going to fall down.
Claire: And is it?
Martin: Usually not. They're more forgiving than people think. What about you?
Claire: Speech and language therapist, NHS, with little ones. So I'm sort of on the floor with toy buses all day trying to get a shy four-year-old to say anything at all. And I love it. The paperwork, less so.
Martin: I'm the same with reports. The interesting part is out on site. The writing up is where it all goes wrong.
Claire: Yes! Do you know what I mean, you've done the actual thing, why do I have to write it all down as well. Sorry. Is that a piano behind you, in your photo?
Martin: My wife Helen's. She teaches music. I don't play, I just get told when I'm humming flat.
Claire: Oh, I sing alto in a choir in Leeds, and I'm terrible at learning my parts. We've got a concert soon and there's one bit I just cannot get, I come in a bar early every single time.
Martin: Helen would say count, and then count again.
Claire: Everyone says that! I'm sure she's right. Erm, I saw your sketch of a bridge, too. Did you do that?
Martin: I did, yes. That's the one at Barcombe, near us. I draw them partly for work and partly for the pleasure of it.
Claire: That's lovely. I do lino prints, the heron and the hare on my board are mine, so the kitchen table's always covered in ink.
Martin: I thought they were rather good, actually. I wondered whether you'd bought them.
Claire: Oh, stop, you'll make me blush. Do you cook? Mark does the Sunday roast, but I do tea in the week, whatever comes in the veg box.
Martin: I do most of our dinners. I tried a Sri Lankan curry last week from a borrowed book. It was nearly right.
Claire: Nearly right is my whole cooking career, love.
calls.C0366:
Claire: Hiya! Oh, hello. Can you hear me alright?
Kerry: Yeah, fine. I'm Kerry.
Claire: Claire. I'm in Otley, near Leeds. Are you up north as well? I'm guessing from the voice.
Kerry: Washington, near Sunderland.
Claire: Oh, lovely. I had a friend at uni from Sunderland, she used to call everyone "pet" and I was so jealous. What do you do?

Kerry: Tia. Staffy. She's eating the settee cushions one at a time.
Claire: Oh no! Mine's Biscuit, a lurcher, and it's socks with him. He takes them in the garden. Gemma's got a lurcher too, did you talk to Gemma?

Claire: No! That's brilliant. Erm, so what do you do when you're not working fifty hours, then?

Claire: Oh, that's a worry, isn't it. My dad's got early dementia, so I'm back and forth to Wakefield helping Mum. Sorry, that's a bit heavy for three minutes.

Claire: Mostly. She's tougher than me. Anyway! Do you do anything arty? I've got ink all over my hands from lino printing.

Claire: Oh, you should go, it's free, and there's a—
Kerry: I know, everyone says.
calls.C0367:
